title.en: Linear First-Order Equations & the Integrating Factor

body.en: Chapter 1's method only handles equations whose right-hand side factors as \( f(x)g(y) \). Many first-order equations don't — including many that show up whenever a quantity's rate of change depends on the quantity itself AND on some outside input at the same time (a heated object losing heat while also being warmed by a heater; a bank account earning interest while also receiving deposits). Some equations of this shape happen to be separable too; many aren't. This chapter builds a technique — the integrating factor — that handles every equation of this shape, separable or not, whenever its coefficients are continuous.

A first-order equation is linear if it can be written in the standard form \[ \frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)\,y=Q(x) \] for some functions \( P \) and \( Q \) — linear because the left side is a linear combination of \( y \) and \( y' \), with no \( y^2 \), \( \sqrt{y} \), \( \sin y \), or similar.

Linear and separable equations overlap, but neither contains the other. Every homogeneous linear equation \( y'+P(x)y=0 \) is separable, since \( y'=-P(x)y \) already has the form \( f(x)g(y) \) with \( f=-P \), \( g(y)=y \). A nonhomogeneous equation can be separable too — for instance \( y'+2xy=x \) rearranges to \( y'=x(1-2y) \), separable with \( f(x)=x \), \( g(y)=1-2y \), even though \( P(x)=2x \) is genuinely non-constant. In general, though, \( Q(x)-P(x)y \) does not factor into a function of \( x \) times a function of \( y \) — and the method below handles every equation of the standard form, whether or not it happens to be separable too.

Let \( P \) and \( Q \) be continuous on an interval \( I \), and let \[ \mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \] be any antiderivative-exponential of \( P \) (so \( \mu'(x)=P(x)\mu(x)\), and \( \mu(x)>0 \) everywhere on \( I \)). Then a differentiable function \( y(x) \) solves \[ \frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)\,y=Q(x) \] on \( I \) if and only if \[ y(x)=\frac{1}{\mu(x)}\left(\int \mu(x)Q(x)\,dx+C\right) \] for some constant \( C \).

The key computation is the product rule applied to \( \mu(x)y(x) \): \[ \frac{d}{dx}\big[\mu(x)y(x)\big]=\mu'(x)y(x)+\mu(x)y'(x)=P(x)\mu(x)y(x)+\mu(x)y'(x)=\mu(x)\big(y'(x)+P(x)y(x)\big), \] using \( \mu'=P\mu \) in the second step. So, since \( \mu(x)\neq0 \) everywhere on \( I \): \[ y'+Py=Q \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mu(y'+Py)=\mu Q \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{d}{dx}\big[\mu y\big]=\mu Q. \] By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, this last equation holds on \( I \) exactly when \( \mu(x)y(x) \) is an antiderivative of \( \mu(x)Q(x) \) — that is, when \[ \mu(x)y(x)=\int\mu(x)Q(x)\,dx+C \] for some constant \( C \), which is exactly \( y(x)=\dfrac{1}{\mu(x)}\Big(\int\mu(x)Q(x)\,dx+C\Big) \) after dividing by \( \mu(x) \).

value.en: Rewrite as \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x) \) by dividing by the coefficient of \( y' \), on an interval where that coefficient is nonzero and \( P,Q \) come out continuous — a point where it vanishes needs the original, undivided equation examined separately
Compute \( \mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \); any one antiderivative of \( P \) works, so take the constant of integration to be \( 0 \)
The left side collapses to \( (\mu y)' \) by construction (Theorem 2.1's proof) — this is the entire point of \( \mu \)

\( \mu y=\displaystyle\int \mu Q\,dx+C \), then divide by \( \mu \) — unlike separable equations, a linear equation in standard form always has an explicit \( y(x) \) waiting at the end, though the integral may not always reduce to elementary functions

body.en:
Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=e^{-x} \).

Already in standard form with \( P(x)=2 \), so \( \mu(x)=e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x} \). Multiplying through: \[ \big(e^{2x}y\big)'=e^{2x}\cdot e^{-x}=e^{x}. \] Integrating: \( e^{2x}y=e^{x}+C \). Dividing by \( e^{2x} \): \[ y=e^{-x}+Ce^{-2x}. \]

label.en: Worked example 2.B — Solving an initial value problem

body.en:
Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{x}=3x^2 \) for \( x>0 \), with \( y(1)=1 \).

\( P(x)=1/x \), so \( \mu(x)=e^{\int(1/x)\,dx}=e^{\ln x}=x \) (using \( x>0 \)). Multiplying through: \[ (xy)'=x\cdot3x^2=3x^3. \] Integrating: \( xy=\dfrac{3x^4}{4}+C \), so \( y=\dfrac{3x^3}{4}+\dfrac{C}{x} \). Applying \( y(1)=1 \): \( \dfrac34+C=1\Rightarrow C=\dfrac14 \). So \[ y=\frac{3x^3}{4}+\frac{1}{4x}. \]

label.en: Worked example 2.C — Application: a filling tank

body.en:
A tank starts with \( 100 \) L of pure water (no salt). Brine with concentration \( 3 \) kg/L flows in at \( 4 \) L/min; the well-mixed solution flows out at only \( 2 \) L/min, so the volume grows: \( V(t)=100+2t \). Find the amount of salt \( y(t) \), and evaluate it at \( t=100 \) minutes, assuming the tank has at least \( 300 \) L of capacity — exactly \( V(100) \) — so it never overflows during that time and the stated flow rates stay valid throughout.

Salt balance: \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=(\text{rate in})-(\text{rate out})=4(3)-2\cdot\dfrac{y}{100+2t}=12-\dfrac{y}{50+t} \) — genuinely linear (\( P(t)=1/(50+t) \) isn't constant), and not separable, since \( 12-\dfrac{y}{50+t} \) doesn't factor into a function of \( t \) times a function of \( y \).

In standard form: \[ \frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{y}{50+t}=12. \] \( \mu(t)=e^{\int dt/(50+t)}=e^{\ln(50+t)}=50+t \) (positive for \( t\ge0 \)). Multiplying through: \[ \big((50+t)y\big)'=12(50+t). \] Integrating: \( (50+t)y=6(50+t)^2+C \), so \( y=6(50+t)+\dfrac{C}{50+t} \). Applying \( y(0)=0 \) (starts as pure water): \( 300+\dfrac{C}{50}=0\Rightarrow C=-15000 \). So \[ y(t)=6(50+t)-\frac{15000}{50+t}, \] and \( y(100)=6(150)-\dfrac{15000}{150}=900-100=800 \) kg.

title.en: ⊙ Explorer · dy/dx + ky = b (constant-coefficient linear equation)

ariaLabel.en: The exact solution curve of dy/dx plus k times y equals b, starting from an adjustable initial value, approaching its steady state b over k

caption.en: Sample points along the solution curve y = b/k + (y0 − b/k)·e^(−kx)

note.en: This is Theorem 2.1 with constant P(x) = k and constant Q(x) = b, the same shape as Worked Example 2.C's filling tank (there, a non-constant P(t) = 1/(50+t)) — the standard form is dy/dx + ky = b, the integrating factor is μ(x) = e^(kx), and carrying out the theorem's formula y = (1/μ)(∫μQ dx + C) with y(0) = y0 gives the exact closed solution y = b/k + (y0 − b/k)·e^(−kx), plotted here without approximation. The amber dot marks the initial point (0, y0); the dashed gray line marks the steady state b/k, the value the curve approaches as x grows since e^(−kx) → 0 for every k > 0 on this slider. Drag y0 above or below b/k and watch the curve approach that same steady state from either side — the transient term (y0 − b/k)·e^(−kx) is the only part that ever changes with x, and it always decays away.

body.en: Separable and linear equations are two of the most important classes of first-order equations, and between Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 2.1 both come with a genuine proof, not a recipe taken on faith. The next stage of this track moves to second-order equations, where a single arbitrary constant is no longer enough to describe every solution.
